learn.hook: A weekly haat under a banyan tree, a busy sabzi mandi, a shiny mall and a shopping app: all of them are markets!
points: A market is any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods and services. It does not have to be a physical place.
Markets by place: weekly markets (haats) that come up on a fixed day, neighbourhood shops, shopping complexes and malls, and online markets on websites and apps.
Wholesale markets (like big mandis) sell goods in large quantities to traders. Retail markets sell in small quantities to the final buyer, the consumer.

Markets by competition: in a competitive market, there are many sellers of similar goods (like a vegetable market). In a monopoly, there is only one seller. In an oligopoly, a few big sellers control the market.
Weekly haats are cheaper for many families because sellers have low costs: they do not pay rent for permanent shops.

example.q: A town has only one company that supplies electricity, and people cannot buy it from anyone else. What kind of market is this?
steps: Buyers have no other choice of seller.
A market with a single seller is a monopoly.

learn.reallife: Before Diwali, your family may buy diyas at a local haat, sweets from a neighbourhood shop and clothes from a mall or an app.

quiz.q: What is a market?
options: Any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange goods and services
A place where only food is sold
quiz.explain: A market can be physical or online; what matters is that buyers and sellers meet to exchange.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a market must be a building

quiz.q: A weekly haat is:
options: A market held on a fixed day of the week
quiz.explain: Haats come up on a particular day in a village or town.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a haat is

quiz.q: A market where goods are sold in large quantities to traders is called a:
quiz.explain: Wholesalers sell in bulk to retailers and other traders.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up wholesale and retail

quiz.q: A market with only one seller is called a:
quiz.explain: 'Mono' means one: a monopoly has a single seller.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up monopoly and oligopoly

quiz.q: A market controlled by a few big sellers is called an:
quiz.explain: 'Oligo' means few: an oligopoly has a few sellers.
quiz.mistake: Confuses few sellers with one seller

quiz.q: Why are goods often cheaper at a weekly haat?
options: Goods there are always of poor quality
Sellers do not pay rent for permanent shops
The government pays for all goods
quiz.explain: Low costs for sellers mean lower prices for buyers.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect sellers' costs with prices

quiz.q: Which is an example of a competitive market?
options: The only water supplier of a town
A town with one electricity company
A vegetable market with many sellers
A single shop with no rivals
quiz.explain: Many sellers offering similar goods compete on price and quality.
quiz.mistake: Picks a single-seller example

quiz.q: Buying a book through a shopping app is an example of:
quiz.explain: Online markets let buyers and sellers trade over the internet.
quiz.mistake: Thinks markets must be physical places

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a market is just a building with shops. Tell him about different types of markets.
teach.praise: Haats, shops, malls, mandis and apps, and markets with one, few or many sellers. Markets are everywhere!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the difference between wholesale and retail?

learn.hook: A tomato travels from a farm to a mandi, to a trader, to a shop and finally to your kitchen. Many hands help it on the way!
points: Between producers and consumers there are often intermediaries (middlemen) such as wholesalers and retailers. They transport, store and sell goods, and each adds to the final price.
In many states, farmers sell crops at regulated markets (mandis) run under Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMCs).

Buyers are called consumers. Consumers have rights: to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal (remedy) and to consumer education. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, protects these rights.
Quality marks help consumers: ISI on many industrial products, AGMARK on farm products like honey and spices, and the BIS Hallmark on gold jewellery.
A seller cannot charge more than the MRP (maximum retail price) printed on a packet. Consumers can complain to consumer commissions or call the National Consumer Helpline (1915).

example.q: Raju bought a packet of chips marked MRP ₹20, but the shopkeeper charged ₹25. What should Raju know?
steps: MRP is the maximum retail price allowed.
Charging ₹25 is more than the MRP, which is not allowed.
Raju can refuse to pay extra and can complain, for example to the National Consumer Helpline.
example.answer: He should pay no more than ₹20 and can complain if overcharged.

learn.reallife: Next time you buy honey or a pressure cooker at home, look for the AGMARK or ISI mark on the label.

quiz.q: Who is a consumer?
options: A person who buys goods or services for use
Only a person who makes goods
quiz.explain: Consumers buy and use goods and services.
quiz.mistake: Confuses consumers with producers

quiz.q: Wholesalers and retailers who stand between producers and consumers are called:
quiz.explain: They link producers to consumers, transporting and selling goods.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for middlemen

quiz.q: What does MRP stand for?
quiz.explain: MRP is the highest price at which a product may be sold to a consumer.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the expansion

quiz.q: Which mark should you look for on honey and spices?
quiz.explain: AGMARK is the quality mark for agricultural products.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the quality marks

quiz.q: A gold necklace with the BIS Hallmark tells you:
options: Its gold purity has been certified
quiz.explain: The Hallmark certifies the purity of gold and silver jewellery.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what Hallmark means

quiz.q: Which law protects consumer rights in India today?
quiz.explain: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sets out consumer rights and how to seek remedies.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other laws

quiz.q: Which number can consumers call for the National Consumer Helpline?
quiz.explain: 1915 is the National Consumer Helpline. 108 is for ambulances and 1098 is the child helpline.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up helpline numbers

quiz.q: Why do intermediaries add to the final price of goods?
options: They lower the price to zero
They have costs like transport and storage and need to earn too
quiz.explain: Each person in the chain adds their costs and earnings to the price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks prices are set only by producers

teach.ask: Gappu was overcharged for birdseed! Tell him who buyers and sellers are and what rights a consumer has.
teach.praise: Consumers have rights, and I can check the MRP and complain if cheated. No more overpaying!
teach.nudge: Good! What can a consumer do if a shopkeeper charges more than the MRP?

learn.hook: When mangoes first arrive in April they are costly; by June, when carts are full of mangoes, prices fall. Why?
points: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices.
Law of demand: when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it; when the price falls, they buy more (other things staying the same).
Supply is the quantity that sellers are willing to sell at different prices. Law of supply: when the price rises, sellers usually offer more; when it falls, they offer less.
The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied is called the equilibrium (market) price.
If supply is very large compared with demand, prices fall; if demand is much larger than supply, prices rise. Weather, festivals and seasons can shift demand and supply.

example.q: A fruit seller finds: at ₹40 a kg people buy 50 kg of mangoes a day; at ₹60, 35 kg; at ₹80, 20 kg; at ₹100, 10 kg. What pattern does this show?
steps: As the price goes up from ₹40 to ₹100, the quantity bought goes down from 50 kg to 10 kg.
This is the law of demand.
example.answer: The law of demand: higher price, less is bought.

learn.reallife: Before Raksha Bandhan, rakhi prices rise because demand jumps for a few days; after the festival, leftover rakhis are sold cheaply.

games.title: Demand and supply: true or false?
items: When the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it.
This is the law of demand.
When the price rises, sellers usually want to sell less.
Higher prices usually encourage sellers to offer more.
At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
That is the definition of equilibrium price.
A huge harvest of tomatoes usually makes tomato prices fall.
More supply than demand pushes prices down.
Festivals can increase the demand for sweets and flowers.
More people want these items during festivals.

items.q: Price rose from ₹40 to ₹55. Rise in ₹?
Sold 20 kg on Mon, 35 kg on Tue. Total kg?
Demand fell from 50 kg to 35 kg. Fall in kg?
4 dozen bananas at ₹50 a dozen costs ₹?

quiz.q: According to the law of demand, when the price of a good rises:
options: People usually buy less of it
People usually buy more of it
quiz.explain: Higher prices usually reduce the quantity demanded.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the law of demand

quiz.q: According to the law of supply, when prices rise, sellers usually:
quiz.explain: Higher prices mean more profit, so sellers supply more.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the law of supply with the law of demand

quiz.q: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is called the:
quiz.explain: At equilibrium price, buyers and sellers agree on the quantity.
quiz.mistake: Confuses market price with the printed MRP

quiz.q: A mango seller finds that people buy 50 kg a day at ₹40 a kg, 35 kg at ₹60, 20 kg at ₹80 and 10 kg at ₹100. How many kg are bought at ₹60 a kg?
quiz.explain: The data shows 35 kg are bought at ₹60.
quiz.mistake: Reads the wrong bar

quiz.q: A mango seller finds that people buy 50 kg a day at ₹40 a kg, 35 kg at ₹60, 20 kg at ₹80 and 10 kg at ₹100. How many fewer kg are bought at ₹100 than at ₹40?
quiz.explain: 50 kg − 10 kg = 40 kg fewer.
quiz.mistake: Uses only one of the two numbers

quiz.q: After a very large onion harvest, what usually happens to onion prices?
quiz.explain: When supply is much larger than demand, prices fall.
quiz.mistake: Does not link more supply with lower prices

quiz.q: Why do flower prices often go up just before a big festival?
quiz.explain: More buyers want flowers at the same time, pushing prices up.
quiz.mistake: Ignores how demand changes with festivals

quiz.q: A shopkeeper buys 10 kg of rice at ₹45 per kg. How much does she pay?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu noticed that mango prices change during the year. Explain demand, supply and price to him.
teach.praise: When many people want something and there is little of it, the price goes up. When there is plenty, it falls. Clever!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the price when there are lots of mangoes but few buyers?
